The Perfect Infinitive can refer to an action that was completed, or that was expected to be completed at some point in the past.

You use the Perfect Infinitive to talk about past actions with verbs like expect, pretend, prefer, or hope.
Example:
She expected to have contacted everyone by the end of the evening.

You use the Perfect Infinitive with non-finite clauses to refer to events that have happened in the past, or events that should or might have happened but did not happen in the end.
A non-finite clause is introduced by a verb with no subject.

Example: To have pulled that off is impressive.
Lots of the customers prefer to have gone elsewhere.
You expect me to have fixed it by the morning?

You use purpose clauses to express the reasons for an action, or the intended motive of a specific situation.
You use words like
to, in order to, so as to or for + -ing to introduce a purpose clause.

Purpose clauses are subordinate to the main clause. The order of the clauses can be interchangeable, as long as the relationship between the two remains clear.
Example:
I have come up with a new plan in order to stay focused.
In order to stay focused, I have come up with a new plan.

You use to with an infinitive as a way to express purpose. We refer to structure as an Infinitive of purpose.
Example: I called to find out if the order had been shipped.

You use in order to or so as to to emphasize an intention or a necessity.
Example:
I would like to call for a meeting in order to / so as to address the current issues in the restaurant.

You use in order that or so that when the second clause starts with a pronoun or a noun.
Example:
You need to give me an answer, so that / in order that I can address the problem quickly.

You also use for + verb -ing to express purpose and intended use.
Example:
These boots are made for walking.
The fridge needs to be up and running by tomorrow morning for receiving our usual deliveries.
In order to fix them I'll need another half day.

images.text:
Vanessa: Hi Jim, what took so long?
Jim: I had to cross hell's half acre to get those hoses. There's only one supplier that carries them. You appear to have managed pretty well without a fridge. To have pulled that off is impressive.
Vanessa: I wish I could say that it had been. Lots of the customers prefer to have gone elsewhere. Some left for the sake of trying the new restaurant down the street.
Jim: That's unfortunate.

Vanessa: Are those hoses going to be easy enough to install? The fridge needs to be up and running by tomorrow morning for receiving our usual deliveries. If we lose any more customers, I'll expect to have been fired by the end of next week.
Jim: Oh dear. There are more issues with this appliance than I thought. In order to fix them I'll need another half day.
Vanessa: Can you work tonight?
Jim: No can do. I was expected to have been home by now. It's 11:30pm? You expect me to have fixed it by the morning?

Vanessa: I have had way too many mishaps and customer complaints. Even some of our loyal customers have abandoned us. It makes me look as though I'm incompetent. What can we do to get back in business?
Jim: First we could go home for sleep, and second we could cut your losses and get you another fridge. This one won't be running forever and some of the parts are next to impossible to get! I can have one in at 8 am. You have my word!
Vanessa: If getting a new fridge is what it's going to take for this restaurant to run smoothly, then we'd better do it. Bill will need to be forewarned, though. Fine. Let's call it a day.
